Something to note, if you're unfamiliar with this, is that there are some folks meandering around with black suit jackets on. They are taking notes, as you may notice. They are the judges and they come from long histories of drum corps and pipe bands. They're all very accomplished players and many of them often have professional experience and world championships under their belts.

But, the judges sometimes haven't had time to watch your practice. So, they sometimes get in the way. If a judge gets in the way, you're to keep the pace and walk over them. You can't have points deducted for doing so. You can literally march right over them.

What they're doing is taking notes about your playing, marching, and difficulty of the score. The marching aspect is very important and you will have precise timing - if you want to do well. It's very much like drilling in the military, and they share the same history. On our side of the pond, a famous fella was John Phillips Sousa - but I don't want to digress too much.

Your lines and steps must be exact. You must step down at the same time, lift at the same time, lift as high as your peers, and maintain equal lines. Even your nose should line up with the nose of the person beside you.

If you drop a stick, you're to keep playing as if you have that stick. Do not miss a beat. Do not make any sign of having dropped (or broken) it. You will continue to play as though you had that stick. If you were to stop and pick up the stick (or even your instrument, should you drop that) then you will absolutely not win the competition. In marching bands, where they have things like color guards, you do not stop to pick up your dropped flag, your dropped instrument, or anything. You keep marching and, funniest of all, you continue to pretend you have the instrument or flag. If you've dropped it, you pretty much play air guitar until your piece is done.

That's true even if you drop a drum stick while twirling it, tossing it, or flourishing. You still continue to drum as though you had that stick. You do not carry extra mallets or sticks with you onto the field. It's not uncommon to see a dropped stick, as it's not easy to march and drum like that at the same time and the added showmanship really compounds the issue. So, if you watch 'em, you'll see them drop their sticks here and there and you'll be able to see 'em pretty much playing air drum.

If you get the chance to go see a drum corps (or a marching band), I highly recommend it. They're cheap (or free) to get into and the band can certainly use your support. It's a great time and there's some really great music played. Sometimes, they don't do traditional music but will do something modern and really throw a lot of energy into the marching aspect. As a bit of a traditionalist, I much prefer a drum and bugle corps over a marching band and I make my tsk face when the marching band has pom-pom girls. Still, it's worth seeing all of 'em. It's a great family activity and a great way to spend a sunny weekend afternoon.
